title: Course Schedule III
description: Maximize the number of courses completed by their deadlines, using a deadline-sorted greedy sweep with a max-heap swap-out.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given courses[i] = [duration, lastDay], meaning a course takes duration consecutive days and must finish on or before lastDay, return the maximum number of courses that can be completed, taken one at a time in some order.

blocks.caption: A max-heap of taken durations lets the single longest course be dropped whenever a deadline is missed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","courses[][] (each [duration, lastDay])"],["Rule","Courses are taken one at a time (no overlap); each must finish by its lastDay"],["Output","Maximum number of courses that can be completed"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Processing courses in order of increasing DEADLINE, and greedily trying to take every one, is the standard approach for deadline-scheduling problems. When a deadline is missed, the greedy fix is to drop the SINGLE LONGEST course taken so far (not necessarily the current one), since that frees up the most time while keeping the same course count.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This "greedily take everything, then swap out the worst choice if something breaks" pattern is common in deadline and budget-constrained scheduling problems, and a max-heap is the natural way to track "the worst choice so far" efficiently.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture courses arriving in order of their deadlines. Take every course tentatively, tracking total elapsed time. If the running total ever exceeds the CURRENT course's deadline, something has to go: dropping the single LONGEST course taken so far (not necessarily the one that just broke the deadline) frees the most time while keeping the same total count of courses taken.

blocks.caption: Dropping the longest course taken so far frees the most time for the same course count.

items: Maintain a max-heap of durations of courses currently "kept," plus a running total time.

For each course: add its duration to the running time and push it to the heap; if the running time now exceeds this course's deadline, pop and discard the LARGEST duration in the heap, subtracting it from the running time.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
courses = [[100,200],[200,1300],[1000,1250],[2000,3200]], sorted by deadline (already in this order).

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final heap has 3 courses, matching the expected output. Course [1000,1250] was tentatively taken but dropped when it broke its own deadline, since it happened to be the longest course at that point.
5. How Should We Think?
A brute-force approach tries every subset (or every ordering) of courses, checking which combination fits all deadlines while maximizing count. This is correct but exponential.

Sorting by deadline first ensures each course is only ever compared against its own deadline using the total time accumulated by courses no later than it. When a deadline is missed, dropping the LONGEST course seen so far (via a max-heap) is provably optimal: it frees the maximum possible time while keeping the course count unchanged, always leaving room to potentially fit a future course.
6. Brute Force Solution
After sorting by deadline, recursively try including or excluding each course, tracking the maximum count of courses that fit within their deadlines.

codes.python:
def schedule_course(courses):
    best = 0
    n = len(courses)

    def backtrack(index, time, count):
        nonlocal best
        best = max(best, count)
        if index == n:
            return
        duration, last_day = courses[index]
        if time + duration <= last_day:
            backtrack(index + 1, time + duration, count + 1)
        backtrack(index + 1, time, count)

    sorted_courses = sorted(courses, key=lambda c: c[1])
    courses[:] = sorted_courses
    backtrack(0, 0, 0)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(schedule_course([[100, 200], [200, 1300], [1000, 1250], [2000, 3200]]))
    print(schedule_course([[1, 2]]))

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Exponential exploration is infeasible beyond small inputs; the greedy max-heap approach achieves the same optimal result in far less time.
8. Optimize the Solution

Sort by deadline. Maintain a max-heap of taken durations and a running total time. For each course, add its duration and push it to the heap; if the running time now exceeds this course's deadline, pop the largest duration from the heap and subtract it from the running time, effectively swapping out the worst previous choice.

items: Sort by lastDay, O(n log n).
For each course, push its duration and update the running time, O(log n).
If the deadline is missed, pop the largest duration (the heap top) and adjust the running time, O(log n).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sorting by deadline is the standard first step for deadline-constrained scheduling problems.
When a greedy "take everything" approach breaks a constraint, swapping out the single worst previous choice (tracked via a max-heap) is a common, provably-safe fix.
This "greedy take, then heap-based swap-out" pattern applies broadly to budget or deadline-constrained selection problems.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Course Schedule III is solved by sorting courses by deadline and greedily taking each one, tracked with a max-heap of durations. Whenever the running time exceeds a course's deadline, dropping the single longest course taken so far frees the maximum possible time, keeping the course count as large as possible, all in O(n log n) time.
